question: What is the main abnormal type of haemoglobin found in sickle cell anaemia?
explanation: You nailed it! Haemoglobin S is the faulty protein that causes red blood cells to change shape when oxygen levels drop. Great start! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells take on a crescent or sickle shape in sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Dehydration causes the bone marrow to manufacture flat instead of round cells
options.B: Excess iron in the bloodstream physically crushes the cells into sharp points
options.C: White blood cells attack the red blood cells and reshape their outer membranes
options.D: Abnormal haemoglobin molecules stick together to form rigid rods when oxygen is low

explanation: Think of it like a chain reaction: when oxygen drops, HbS molecules clump into stiff rods that push the cell into that classic crescent sickle shape. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h1)

question: What kind of genetic inheritance pattern does sickle cell anaemia follow?
explanation: It's autosomal recessive! This means a child needs to inherit two faulty genes—one from each parent—to actually have the disease. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h2)

question: If both parents have the sickle cell trait (AS), what is the chance they will have a child with sickle cell anaemia (SS)?
explanation: Genetics can be tricky, but with AS carriers, there's a 1 in 4 (25%) chance per pregnancy of having an SS child. Knowing this helps us counsel families better! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h2)

question: Why do babies with sickle cell anaemia usually look completely healthy at birth?

options.A: The bone marrow does not produce red blood cells until the age of one
options.B: Infant blood vessels are too wide for blockages to possibly form
options.C: The mother's immune system filters out all the abnormal blood cells
options.D: High levels of fetal haemoglobin protect the red blood cells temporarily

explanation: Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) is tough and resists sickling. It's only when HbF starts dropping after birth that symptoms begin to show up. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h3)

question: What is hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) in young children with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Painful swelling of the hands and feet caused by blocked blood vessels in the small bones
options.B: A temporary paralysis of the lower limbs following a severe viral infection
options.C: Complete loss of sensation in the fingers and toes due to nerve damage
options.D: An abnormal curvature of the foot bones caused by vitamin deficiencies

explanation: Dactylitis is one of the earliest warning signs! Blocked blood flow in tiny hand and foot bones leads to very painful swelling in babies and toddlers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h3)

question: What is the most common reason a patient with sickle cell anaemia is rushed to the emergency ward?
explanation: Spot on. When sickled cells block blood flow, tissues get starved of oxygen, triggering intense pain crises that bring patients straight to the hospital. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h4)

question: Which dangerous emergency involves blood getting trapped inside the spleen, causing a sudden drop in blood volume?
explanation: In splenic sequestration, blood pools massively inside the spleen. This causes the spleen to swell rapidly and puts the patient into shock very quickly. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why is giving plenty of fluids a top nursing priority during a sickle cell pain crisis?

options.A: It decreases blood viscosity, helping sickled cells flow through small vessels
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from filtering out necessary pain medications
options.C: It directly stops the bone marrow from producing abnormal haemoglobin S
options.D: It replaces the white blood cells that are lost during a hemolytic attack

explanation: Hydration is key! Fluids thin out the blood (reduces viscosity), making it much easier for those sticky cells to move through tight blood vessels. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h5)

question: A patient comes in with a severe pain crisis, but their oxygen saturation is completely normal at 98% on room air. What should you do about oxygen therapy?

options.A: Administer high-flow oxygen immediately to reverse the bone pain
options.B: Place the patient on a non-rebreather mask to prevent acute chest syndrome
options.C: Monitor saturation closely and withhold oxygen unless desaturation occurs
options.D: Apply nasal cannula oxygen only during periods of sleep

explanation: If their oxygen level is fine, extra oxygen isn't needed—in fact, it can trick the bone marrow into slowing down red blood cell production. Just keep a close eye on them! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h5)

question: What is the main goal of genetic counseling for couples in communities with high sickle cell rates?

options.A: To test newborns for immediate signs of acute chest syndrome
options.B: To provide accurate information on inheritance risks for family planning
options.C: To administer prophylactic antibiotics to prevent bacterial infections
options.D: To prescribe daily doses of folic acid for blood cell production

explanation: Counseling empowers couples with clear facts about their genotypes so they can make informed, confident family planning choices. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a helpful community health strategy for managing sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Educating the public to dispel myths about spiritual causes
options.B: Encouraging families to hide children with symptoms from public view
options.C: Providing accessible pre-marital genotype screening clinics
options.D: Training primary healthcare nurses to offer basic genetic counseling

explanation: Stigma is harmful! Hiding children only delays vital medical care and isolates them. Community health nursing is all about education, openness, and support. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h6)
